name: Archetype: Bronze Age chariot states

weightNotes.aggression: Annual royal campaigning seasons into the Levant (Thutmose III's campaigns, Ramesses II at Kadesh); kings sought battle and tribute.
weightNotes.maneuver: Chariot mobility on open ground allowed fast strikes: at Kadesh (c. 1274 BC) Hittite chariotry crossed the river and hit the Egyptian Ra division on the march. Infantry-bound sieges pull it back to mid.
weightNotes.flanking: Chariot wings struck columns and flanks (Kadesh), but battle lines were simple; mid.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Campaigns aimed at city-states; Megiddo (15th c. BC) fell after a seven-month blockade with a moat and palisade rather than by assault. Field battle and blockade both common; just under mid.
weightNotes.reserveUse: At Kadesh Muwatalli II still held a large reserve of chariotry and infantry and sent another thousand chariots in a second wave; only partial evidence elsewhere.
weightNotes.scouting: Kadesh: Ramesses was misled by two captured nomads who were Hittite spies, and camped unaware of the enemy army behind Old Kadesh. Low.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Low-cohesion levy infantry and small elite chariot corps; armies broke quickly once the chariot arm was beaten. Educated guess anchored on ancient rout behaviour (Sabin 2000); grade C.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Chariots (archer platforms) with infantry runners and spearmen; Drews argues chariots were the decisive arm and infantry auxiliary, so integration was limited.
weightNotes.initiative: Command centred on the king in his chariot; outcomes followed his person (Ramesses at Kadesh). Low.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Egyptian campaigns used coastal harbours and requisitioned harvests (Megiddo); chariots needed fodder and repair, tying armies to supply. Mid.

summary: Palace states (New Kingdom Egypt, Hittites, Mitanni, Mycenaean and Levantine kingdoms) fielded expensive elite chariot corps, each vehicle carrying a driver and a composite-bow archer (Hittite chariots three men), supported by levied and professional infantry. Kings campaigned each season against city-states; battles were won by massed chariot archery and charges on open ground, and cities taken by blockade.
whyItWorked: The chariot gave a stable, fast archery platform that out-shot and out-ran infantry on open ground, and only palace economies could afford horses, bows and specialist crews, so chariot states dominated their regions for centuries.
whereItFailed: Poor intelligence and march security: Kadesh, where Ramesses II was surprised in camp. Chariots were costly, fragile and useless on broken ground or against walls (Megiddo needed seven months). In the Late Bronze Age collapse (c. 1200 BC) chariot states fell to raiders and infantry, which Drews attributes to massed skirmishing infantry defeating chariot armies.

sources.title: Battle of Megiddo (15th century BC), Wikipedia
